bibl.title: Driving fast-spiking cells induces gamma rhythm and controls sensory responses

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Whether driving one cortical cell type is enough to create a network rhythm, and what that rhythm then does to sensory transmission.
span.quote: We causally tested these hypotheses in barrel cortex in vivo by targeting optogenetic manipulation selectively to fast-spiking interneurons.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Our data directly support the fast-spiking-gamma hypothesis and provide the first causal evidence that distinct network activity states can be induced in vivo by cell-type-specific activation.

span.label: cortical gamma oscillations
span.quote: Cortical gamma oscillations (20–80 Hz) predict increases in focused attention, and failure in gamma regulation is a hallmark of neurological and psychiatric disease.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We causally tested these hypotheses in barrel cortex in vivo by targeting optogenetic manipulation selectively to fast-spiking interneurons.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Rhythmic FS-generated IPSPs gate sensory transmission: inhibition blocks input at its peak and releases it during decay, temporally sharpening cortical responses
span.quote: Our results indicate that the rhythmic, FS-induced IPSP restricts sensory transmission during its peak, and permits transmission after its decay, leading to a temporal sharpening of cortical sensory responses

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Increased FS firing recruits a resonance in the surrounding cortical network whose preferred band is set by the circuit's synaptic and biophysical properties
span.quote: One possible explanation for these results is that increased FS firing recruits resonant gamma-range activity in the surrounding local network as a function of the synaptic and biophysical properties of the cortical circuit.

span.label: Synchronous inhibition from fast-spiking cells opens a narrow window in which excitation is effective, which is what synchronises the ensemble
span.quote: Current theory predicts that gamma oscillations are generated by synchronous activity of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons, with the resulting rhythmic inhibition producing neural ensemble synchrony by generating a narrow window for effective excitation.

span.label: The gamma band is a property of the circuit rather than of the drive: changing light intensity changes how much amplification occurs but not which frequencies are amplified
span.quote: Whereas drive affected the amplitude of enhancement, LFP power was selectively amplified within the gamma range regardless of light intensity or spike probability ( Fig. 3h ), indicating that the gamma oscillations evoked by FS activity are a resonant circuit property.

span.label: Stimulating at random frequencies still produces gamma, so the rhythm is emergent and does not have to be imposed
span.quote: In addition, randomly patterned light stimulation of FS cells with frequencies evenly distributed across a broad range evoked a significant increase in LFP power specific to the gamma range ( n =7 sites in 4 animals; P <0.05; Supplementary Fig. 7 ), further indicating that FS-evoked gamma oscillations are an emergent property of the circuit and do not require exclusive drive in the gamma range.

span.label: The induced rhythm still needs excitatory feedback - blocking glutamate receptors abolishes it even while the interneurons keep firing
span.quote: Furthermore, light-induced gamma oscillations were largely eliminated by blocking AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) and NMDA ( N -methyl- d -aspartate) receptors, despite high levels of evoked FS firing ( n =4 sites in 4 animals; P <0.01; Supplementary Fig. 9 ).

span.label: The functional consequence: inhibition blocks input at its peak and permits it after decay, which sharpens the timing of sensory responses
span.quote: Our results indicate that the rhythmic, FS-induced IPSP restricts sensory transmission during its peak, and permits transmission after its decay, leading to a temporal sharpening of cortical sensory responses ( Fig. 4g ).

span.label: Cell-type targeting works through Cre-dependent expression, so the light acts only on neurons that already carry the driver
span.quote: We targeted expression of ChR2 specifically to parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking (FS-PV + ) interneurons by injecting the adeno-associated viral vector double-floxed inverted open reading frame ChR2–mCherry (AAV DIO ChR2–mCherry ), with Cre-dependent expression of ChR2, into PV–Cre knock-in mice ( Fig. 1a , Supplementary Figs 1 and 2 and Methods )

span.label: The effect was not obtained in layer 5, so the result is confined to the layers where activation was observed
span.note: what this limits: the laminar scope of the effect: WE DID NOT OBSERVE LIGHT ACTIVATION OF LAYER 5 FS CELLS (n=12 SITES IN 7 ANIMALS)
span.quote: We did not observe light activation of layer 5 FS cells ( n =12 sites in 7 animals).

span.label: Labelling efficiency falls off with distance from the injection, so the manipulated population is not uniform across the field
span.note: what this limits: what 'the PV population' means at any distance from the injection: THE LABELLING EFFICIENCY OF AAV DIO ChR2-mCHERRY VARIED OVER DISTANCE FROM THE INJECTION SITE; CLOSE TO THE CENTRE OF THE INJECTION, >97% OF THE PV+ INTERNEURONS EXPRESSED ChR2-mCHERRY
span.quote: The labelling efficiency of AAV DIO ChR2–mCherry varied over distance from the injection site; close to the centre of the injection, >97% of the PV + interneurons expressed ChR2–mCherry.

span.label: The excitatory comparison covers at most half the target population, against near-complete coverage on the inhibitory side
span.note: about this quote: 2026-08-25 terminal-a. FLATTENED EXPONENT IN THIS QUOTE - THE NUMBER IS WRONG BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE AS IT STANDS. The staged text reads '8.4×10 6', where the paper writes 10 to the power 6. The superscript was pushed onto the line by the PDF extractor. The quote is verbatim to the staged text and its anchor is sound; the STAGED TEXT is what is damaged. NOT repaired - repair means re-staging the body and re-anchoring the record. Found by CLAUDE_B, row chk_flattened_exponent_in_a_quote. · what this limits: the excitatory arm of the FS-versus-RS comparison, which is covered less completely than the inhibitory arm: AT LEAST 50% OF THE aCamKII+ NEURONS IN LAYER 2/3 EXPRESSED ChR2-mCHERRY (913 OF 1,638 CELLS)
span.quote: At least 50% of the αCamKII + neurons in layer 2/3 expressed ChR2–mCherry (913 of 1,638 cells in a total area of 8.4×10 6 μm 3 ) close to the injection site, covering an anterioposterior distance of 1,560±154.9 μm (mean±s.d., n =3).

span.label: The pyramidal-drive comparison at 40 Hz produced a small increase that did not reach significance, so the dissociation is asymmetric in strength
span.note: what this limits: the frequency specificity of the dissociation: RS STIMULATION AT 8 Hz CAUSED A SIGNIFICANT INCREASE OF LFP POWER AT 8 Hz (P<0.001), WHEREAS RS STIMULATION AT 40 Hz CAUSED ONLY A SMALL, NONSIGNIFICANT INCREASE IN 40-Hz LFP POWER
span.quote: In contrast, stimulation of RS cells at 8 Hz in the αCamKII–Cre mice caused a significant increase of LFP power at 8 Hz ( P <0.001), whereas RS stimulation at 40 Hz caused only a small, nonsignificant increase in 40-Hz LFP power ( Fig. 3f ).

span.label: The phase-gating experiment rests on twenty cells in three animals
span.note: what this limits: the phase-gating result: n=20 CELLS IN 3 ANIMALS, responses to a single vibrissa deflection at one of five phases relative to a single gamma cycle
span.quote: To test this hypothesis directly, we stimulated FS cells at 40 Hz with light pulses to establish gamma oscillations, and recorded the responses of RS cells to a single vibrissa deflection presented at one of five phases relative to a single gamma cycle ( n =20 cells in 3 animals; Fig. 4a ).

span.label: a microbial light-sensitive cation channel is imported as the tool for driving a specific mammalian cortical cell type in vivo
span.quote: we used the light-sensitive bacteriorhodopsin Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), a cation channel activated by ~470 nm blue light

span.label: each imaging channel collected in MULTI-TRACK mode rather than simultaneously
span.note: eliminates: optical cross-talk between channels - bleed from one fluorophore into another channel would appear as co-labelling that is not there
span.quote: Scans from each channel were collected in multi-track mode to avoid cross-talk between channels.

span.label: gamma oscillations
span.quote: Here we show that light-driven activation of fast-spiking interneurons at varied frequencies (8–200 Hz) selectively amplifies gamma oscillations.

span.label: fast-spiking
span.quote: Here we show that light-driven activation of fast-spiking interneurons at varied frequencies (8–200 Hz) selectively amplifies gamma oscillations.

span.label: the causal claim - SUFFICIENCY: driving fast-spiking cells is enough to produce gamma, which is what the optogenetic activation shows
span.quote: This double dissociation of cell-type-specific state induction (gamma by FS and lower frequencies by RS) directly supports the prediction that FS-PV + interneuron activation is sufficient and specific for induction of gamma oscillations

span.label: the causal claim - NECESSITY: naturally occurring gamma depends on the same cells, shown by shifting its phase with a single pulse
span.quote: We found that brief FS activation shifted the phase of both spontaneously occurring gamma oscillations ( n =26 trials, 4 animals; Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; P <0.01; Fig. 3i ) and those evoked by midbrain reticular formation stimulation ( n =18 trials, 2 animals; P <0.05; Supplementary Fig. 8 ).

span.label: gamma - INDUCED by light: the rhythm created by driving interneurons, which is what most of the paper measures
span.quote: Driving FS cells at 40 Hz caused a specific increase in the 35–40 Hz frequency band in the LFP ( Fig. 3c and Supplementary Figs 5 and 6 ).

span.label: gamma - NATURALLY occurring: the spontaneous rhythm, a different object that the induced one is shown to connect with
span.quote: To test whether intrinsically occurring gamma oscillations show a similar dependence on FS activity, we gave single light pulses during epochs of natural gamma.

span.label: the frequency band - as set by the DRIVE: the alternative in which spike probability determines which band is enhanced
span.quote: Alternatively, the increase in gamma activity may result from the specific level of evoked FS spiking, and changing spiking probability would shift the frequency of the enhanced LFP band.

span.label: the frequency band - as set by the CIRCUIT: resonance, which is what varying light intensity showed
span.quote: One possible explanation for these results is that increased FS firing recruits resonant gamma-range activity in the surrounding local network as a function of the synaptic and biophysical properties of the cortical circuit.

span.label: builds-on → the fast-spiking-gamma hypothesis (prior computational models and recordings holding that gamma is generated by synchronous fast-spiking interneuron activity)
span.quote: Our data directly support the fast-spiking-gamma hypothesis and provide the first causal evidence that distinct network activity states can be induced in vivo by cell-type-specific activation.

span.label: supports → the fast-spiking-gamma hypothesis derived from computational modelling
span.quote: Computational modelling indicates that this synchronous activity is sufficient to induce 20–80-Hz oscillations that are stabilized and regulated by fast excitatory feedback from pyramidal neurons

span.label: supports → the account of gamma as gating synaptic input rhythmically to synchronise cell assemblies
span.quote: The cyclical FS inhibition underlying gamma oscillations is believed to cause this synchrony by rhythmically gating synaptic inputs

span.label: extends → prior in vivo recordings showing sensory-evoked gamma and phase-locked pyramidal firing
span.quote: Cortical recordings in vivo show sensory-evoked gamma oscillations in the local field potential (LFP) and phase-locked firingof excitatorypyramidal cells,indicating entrainmentof excitatory neurons to rhythmic inhibitory activity 9 , 13 – 15 .

span.label: fast-spiking —causes→ gamma oscillations
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Here we show that light-driven activation of fast-spiking interneurons at varied frequencies (8–200 Hz) selectively amplifies gamma oscillations.

span.label: regular spiking —distinct-from→ gamma oscillations
span.quote: In contrast, pyramidal neuron activation amplifies only lower frequency oscillations, a cell-type-specific double dissociation.

span.label: fast-spiking —causes→ inhibitory postsynaptic potentials
span.quote: We found that a 1-ms light pulse was sufficient to evoke large, fast IPSPs, confirming direct synaptic inhibition of RS cells by light-activated FS cells ( Fig. 2b ).

span.label: inhibitory postsynaptic potentials —causes→ precision
span.quote: Our results indicate that the rhythmic, FS-induced IPSP restricts sensory transmission during its peak, and permits transmission after its decay, leading to a temporal sharpening of cortical sensory responses ( Fig. 4g ).

span.label: phase —causes→ precision
span.quote: The precision of sensory-evoked spikes was significantly enhanced in a gamma-phase-dependent manner ( P <0.01; Fig. 4f ).

span.label: AMPA —causes→ gamma oscillations
span.quote: Furthermore, light-induced gamma oscillations were largely eliminated by blocking AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) and NMDA ( N -methyl- d -aspartate) receptors, despite high levels of evoked FS firing ( n =4 sites in 4 animals; P <0.01; Supplementary Fig. 9 ).

span.label: resonant circuit property —contrasted-with→ spike probability
span.quote: Whereas drive affected the amplitude of enhancement, LFP power was selectively amplified within the gamma range regardless of light intensity or spike probability ( Fig. 3h ), indicating that the gamma oscillations evoked by FS activity are a resonant circuit property.

span.label: channelrhodopsin-2 —operationalised-as→ optogenetic
span.quote: To test directly the hypothesis that FS interneuron activity in an in vivo cortical circuit is sufficient to induce gamma oscillations, we used the light-sensitive bacteriorhodopsin Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), a cation channel activated by ~470 nm blue light

span.label: Cre —operationalised-as→ parvalbumin
span.quote: We targeted expression of ChR2 specifically to parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking (FS-PV + ) interneurons by injecting the adeno-associated viral vector double-floxed inverted open reading frame ChR2–mCherry (AAV DIO ChR2–mCherry ), with Cre-dependent expression of ChR2, into PV–Cre knock-in mice ( Fig. 1a , Supplementary Figs 1 and 2 and Methods ) 18 , 19 .

span.label: parvalbumin —part-of→ fast-spiking
span.quote: We targeted expression of ChR2 specifically to parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking (FS-PV + ) interneurons by injecting the adeno-associated viral vector double-floxed inverted open reading frame ChR2–mCherry (AAV DIO ChR2–mCherry ), with Cre-dependent expression of ChR2, into PV–Cre knock-in mice ( Fig. 1a , Supplementary Figs 1 and 2 and Methods )

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED FROM A NEITHER-ENDPOINT SPAN) · local field potential —operationalised-as→ gamma oscillations
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED FROM A NEITHER-ENDPOINT SPAN. The old span stated a prediction about light pulses and named neither term. This sentence names both and states where the one is measured in the other: 'sensory-evoked GAMMA OSCILLATIONS in the LOCAL FIELD POTENTIAL (LFP)'. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Cortical recordings in vivo show sensory-evoked gamma oscillations in the local field potential (LFP) and phase-locked firingof excitatorypyramidal cells,indicating entrainmentof excitatory neurons to rhythmic inhibitory activity 9 , 13 – 15 .

span.label: double dissociation —operationalised-as→ fast-spiking
span.quote: This double dissociation of cell-type-specific state induction (gamma by FS and lower frequencies by RS) directly supports the prediction that FS-PV + interneuron activation is sufficient and specific for induction of gamma oscillations

span.label: vibrissa —part-of→ barrel cortex
span.quote: Barrel cortex, which processes information from the rodent vibrissae (whiskers), was targeted as a well-defined model of basic sensory cortical function.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Stimulation of FS cells at 8 Hz in the PV–Cre mice had no effect on LFP power at 8 Hz, but FS stimulation at 40 Hz caused a significant increase in 40-Hz LFP power (paired t -test; P <0.001; Fig. 3e )

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: The presence of gamma oscillations significantly decreased the amplitude of the RS sensory response at three phase points, consistent with the enhanced level of overall inhibition in this state ( P <0.05; 1-way ANOVA with Dunnett's post-test; Fig. 4d )

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
span.quote: We found that brief FS activation shifted the phase of both spontaneously occurring gamma oscillations ( n =26 trials, 4 animals; Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; P <0.01; Fig. 3i )

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: All numbers are given as mean ± s.e.m., except where otherwise noted.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that 96.7±1.0% (mean±s.d., n =4,234 ChR2–mCherry + neurons, 4 animals) of the ChR2–mCherry + neurons expressed PV

span.label: Optogenetically driving fast-spiking interneurons across a wide frequency range amplified oscillations selectively in the gamma band.
span.quote: Here we show that light-driven activation of fast-spiking interneurons at varied frequencies (8–200 Hz) selectively amplifies gamma oscillations.

span.label: Driving FS cells within 20–80 Hz significantly increased local field potential power at those frequencies, whereas lower-frequency drive did not.
span.quote: We found that activation of FS cells in the 20–80 Hz range resulted in significant amplification of LFP power at those frequencies

span.label: Gamma-band amplification persisted regardless of stimulation intensity or evoked spike probability, indicating gamma is a resonant property of the local circuit rather than a copy of the drive.
span.quote: Whereas drive affected the amplitude of enhancement, LFP power was selectively amplified within the gamma range regardless of light intensity or spike probability

span.label: A single 1-ms light pulse to FS cells produced large fast IPSPs in nearby regular-spiking neurons, confirming direct monosynaptic inhibition.
span.quote: We found that a 1-ms light pulse was sufficient to evoke large, fast IPSPs, confirming direct synaptic inhibition of RS cells by light-activated FS cells

span.label: Activating FS cells suppressed whisker-evoked responses in neighbouring excitatory neurons.
span.quote: Consistent with IPSP induction, activation of FS cells blocked vibrissa-evoked responses in neighbouring RS cells

span.label: The phase of the gamma cycle at which a whisker deflection arrived determined the amplitude, latency and temporal precision of the resulting cortical response.
span.quote: The timing of vibrissa-induced RS action potentials relative to light-evoked inhibition and the gamma cycle had a significant impact on the amplitude, timing and precision of the sensory-evoked responses of RS cells

span.label: Light-induced gamma depended on fast excitatory synaptic transmission, since blocking AMPA and NMDA receptors abolished it even while FS cells still fired strongly.
span.quote: Furthermore, light-induced gamma oscillations were largely eliminated by blocking AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) and NMDA ( N -methyl- d -aspartate) receptors, despite high levels of evoked FS firing

span.label: A brief FS activation reset the phase of spontaneously occurring gamma oscillations, linking naturally occurring gamma to FS activity.
span.quote: We found that brief FS activation shifted the phase of both spontaneously occurring gamma oscillations ( n =26 trials, 4 animals; Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; P <0.01; Fig. 3i )

span.label: driving fast-spiking interneurons amplified the local field potential selectively in the 20-80 Hz band
span.quote: We found that activation of FS cells in the 20–80 Hz range resulted in significant amplification of LFP power at those frequencies ( n =14 sites in 6 animals; Fig. 3d ).

span.label: driving excitatory neurons amplified only the lower frequencies, giving a double dissociation by cell type
span.quote: In contrast, 8–24 Hz light activation of RS cells in αCamKII–Cre mice induced increased LFP power at these frequencies, but RS activation at higher frequencies did not affect LFP power ( n =13 sites in 5 mice; Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 5 ).

span.label: the amplified band did not move with light intensity or spike probability, so it is set by the circuit
span.quote: Whereas drive affected the amplitude of enhancement, LFP power was selectively amplified within the gamma range regardless of light intensity or spike probability ( Fig. 3h ), indicating that the gamma oscillations evoked by FS activity are a resonant circuit property.

span.label: single pulses shifted the phase of naturally occurring gamma, linking the induced rhythm to the spontaneous one
span.quote: We found that brief FS activation shifted the phase of both spontaneously occurring gamma oscillations ( n =26 trials, 4 animals; Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; P <0.01; Fig. 3i ) and those evoked by midbrain reticular formation stimulation ( n =18 trials, 2 animals; P <0.05; Supplementary Fig. 8 ).

span.label: the position of a whisker deflection within the gamma cycle changed the amplitude, latency and precision of the response
span.quote: The timing of vibrissa-induced RS action potentials relative to light-evoked inhibition and the gamma cycle had a significant impact on the amplitude, timing and precision of the sensory-evoked responses of RS cells ( Fig. 4b, c ).

span.label: activating the interneurons blocked whisker-evoked responses in neighbouring excitatory cells
span.quote: Consistent with IPSP induction, activation of FS cells blocked vibrissa-evoked responses in neighbouring RS cells ( Fig. 2d, e ; n =6 sites in 5 PV–Cre mice).

span.label: channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2)
span.quote: we used the light-sensitive bacteriorhodopsin Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), a cation channel activated by ~470 nm blue light

span.label: cortical gamma oscillations (20–80 Hz)
span.quote: Cortical gamma oscillations (20–80 Hz) predict increases in focused attention, and failure in gamma regulation is a hallmark of neurological and psychiatric disease.

span.quote: To test this hypothesis, we drove cortical FS cell spiking in virus-transduced PV–Cre mice at a range of frequencies (8–200 Hz) with 1-ms light pulses.

span.label: cell type driven (fast-spiking PV+ interneurons vs regular-spiking excitatory neurons)
span.term: cell type driven (fast-spiking PV+ interneurons vs regular-spiking excitatory neurons)
span.quote: To highlight this distinction, we compared the effects of stimulating the two cell types at 8 and 40 Hz.

span.label: light intensity of the stimulation
span.quote: To discriminate between these possibilities, we stimulated FS cells at varying levels of light intensity.

span.quote: The precise timing of the whisker deflection relative to the light pulses was varied across five phase points.

span.label: relative LFP power in an 8-Hz band around the stimulation frequency
span.term: relative LFP power in an 8-Hz band around the stimulation frequency
span.quote: For each stimulation frequency, we measured the relative power in an 8-Hz band centred on that frequency.

span.label: spike probability per light cycle

span.quote: We recorded light-activated FS and regular spiking (RS) single units in layers 2/3 and 4 of barrel cortex in PV–Cre ( n =64 FS cells in 15 animals) and αCamKII–Cre ( n =56 RS cells in 7 animals) mice.

span.label: 96.7±1.0% — proportion of ChR2-mCherry-expressing neurons that were parvalbumin-positive, confirming targeting specificity
span.quote: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that 96.7±1.0% (mean±s.d., n =4,234 ChR2–mCherry + neurons, 4 animals) of the ChR2–mCherry + neurons expressed PV

span.label: −67.6±1.9 mV — mean reversal potential of the light-evoked IPSPs, consistent with a GABA-A chloride conductance
span.quote: The mean reversal potential of the evoked IPSPs (see Supplementary Methods ) was −67.6±1.9 mV, indicating a GABA A -mediated Cl − conductance characteristic of FS synapses.

span.label: 2.7±1.0 mV — mean peak amplitude of the light-evoked IPSP measured near −55 to −60 mV
span.quote: Mean IPSP peak amplitude at membrane potentials of −55 to −60 mV was 2.7±1.0 mV.

span.label: 0.5 to 0.75 ms — lead time by which light-evoked FS spikes preceded the onset of the postsynaptic IPSP
span.quote: with FS spikes preceding IPSP onset by 0.5 to 0.75 ms

span.label: n =64 FS cells in 15 animals — number of fast-spiking single units recorded in PV–Cre mice (against 56 RS cells in 7 αCamKII–Cre mice)
span.quote: We recorded light-activated FS and regular spiking (RS) single units in layers 2/3 and 4 of barrel cortex in PV–Cre ( n =64 FS cells in 15 animals) and αCamKII–Cre ( n =56 RS cells in 7 animals) mice.

span.label: 9.1 ± 0.08 ms — onset latency of layer 4 regular-spiking responses to whisker deflection
span.quote: Vibrissa stimulations evoked layer 4 RS spike responses with an onset latency of 9.1 ± 0.08 ms.

span.label: 96.7±1.0% — specificity of the targeting - labelled cells that really were parvalbumin-positive
span.quote: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that 96.7±1.0% (mean±s.d., n =4,234 ChR2–mCherry + neurons, 4 animals) of the ChR2–mCherry + neurons expressed PV ( Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Fig. 2 ), and almost all expressed the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid; Supplementary Fig. 3 ) 20 – 23 .

span.label: 0.5 to 0.75 ms — how far the interneuron spike preceded the inhibitory potential it caused
span.quote: The latencies of the presynaptic light-evoked FS spikes agreed well with the onset times of the postsynaptic IPSPs, with FS spikes preceding IPSP onset by 0.5 to 0.75 ms ( Fig. 2c ).
